question: How should general ledger, budgeting and actual-versus-budget data be modelled dimensionally?
contributions: G/L periodic snapshot plus journal-entry transaction schemas
Net-change grain for budget facts and the budget-commitment-payment chain
Consolidated actual-vs-budget fact table and its limits

results.claim: Worked example of net-change budget grain: an original budget of 200,000 is followed by a 40,000 increase in June and a negative 25,000 in October, each stored as a separate fact row.
results.setup: Budget fact table at net-change grain per budget line item, G/L account, organization and effective month (Fig 7.3)
results.quote: have another row in June for a $40,000 increase and then another in October
results.note: October row is negative $25,000; summing all rows to date gives the current approved budget (215,000 by arithmetic, not printed).

results.claim: A company may have 13 four-week accounting periods in a fiscal year starting September 1 instead of 12 calendar months, so fiscal periods need their own treatment.
results.setup: Illustration of fiscal calendar misaligned with Gregorian months
results.quote: a company may have 13 four-week accounting periods

results.claim: A subsidiary fiscal period dimension would hold about 36 fiscal periods for three years times the number of unique calendars.
results.metric: rows in subsidiary fiscal period dimension per calendar
results.setup: Third option for many subsidiary-specific fiscal calendars
results.quote: (approximately 36 for three years) times the number of unique calendars.

results.claim: Account numbers 1,000 through 1,999 might be assets and 2,000 to 2,999 liabilities, so account type should be a dimension attribute rather than a filter on the first digit.
results.setup: Chart of accounts as an intelligent key
results.quote: might be asset accounts, whereas account numbers ranging from 2,000 to 2,999

results.claim: To-date (QTD/YTD) columns should not be stored in fact tables because they are not true to the grain and overstate results when summed; compute them in the access application.
results.quote: In general, to-date totals should be calculated, not stored in the fact table.

limits: 2002 text: references Oracle variable-width columns, bit-mapped indexes and OLAP cube vendors as then-current; modern columnar warehouses change several trade-offs.
No data or measurements; design advice only.
Consolidated fact tables are a dimensionality compromise at the least common denominator of dimensions (p.184).
Defers budgeting chain detail to Adamson and Venerable, Data Warehouse Design Solutions (Wiley 1998).
practices: Pair a G/L periodic snapshot (grain: one row per accounting period per lowest-level chart-of-accounts account) with a journal-entry transaction fact table (p.175-178).
Split the chart of accounts into a G/L account dimension and an organization roll-up dimension; add a separate G/L (books) dimension when multiple sets of books exist (p.175-176).
Use bridge tables from Chapter 6 for ragged organization hierarchies; handle fixed-depth hierarchies as attributes (p.176).
Store the period-end balance as a semiadditive fact because otherwise balances need recomputing from the beginning of time (p.176).
Do not store quarter-to-date or year-to-date facts; calculate them in the data access application or via roll-up attributes on the period dimension (p.177, 184).
For multiple currencies hold both local and corporate-currency amounts per row and a currency foreign key (p.177).
Treat the journal entry number as a degenerate dimension; use a single amount with a debit/credit indicator, and a two-row decode dimension or DR/CR abbreviation (p.178-179).
For one fiscal calendar, make fiscal periods hierarchical attributes of the daily date dimension; for few calendars, add labelled attribute sets to one date dimension (p.179).

For many fiscal calendars, use a date-by-subsidiary outrigger exposed through a view, separate physical date dimensions sharing surrogate keys, or a subsidiary fiscal period foreign key in the fact table (p.179-180).
Do not replace the operational system's official financial statements; optionally build an aggregated financial statement database by period and cost center (p.180).
Set budget fact grain to the net change of a line item in a cost center per month, not a monthly status snapshot, so the single budget amount is fully additive (p.181-182).
Model budget, commitments and payments as a chain of fact tables with growing dimension lists and combine them by drill-across (p.183).
Replicate the category name into the subcategory column for uneven hierarchies to avoid a Not Applicable bucket (p.182).
Build a consolidated actual-vs-budget fact table only when the facts share grain and dimensionality; do not force-fit with artificial facts or dimensions (p.184-185).
Show actuals at both effective and planned currency conversion rates so remote managers are not penalised for rate changes (p.184).
Conform dimensions across the warehouse even when buying packaged analytic solutions (p.186).

terms.definition: The cornerstone of the G/L, an intelligent key usually consisting of a series of identifiers.
A fact such as a balance that is not additive across all dimensions (here, over time).
Budget fact grain: the change to a budget line item in a cost center during the month; summing over time gives the current approved budget.
Fact tables that combine metrics at a common granularity.
An identifier such as the journal entry number kept in the fact table with no dimension table.
A table keyed by date and subsidiary holding subsidiary-specific fiscal groupings.
